catalog_citation: Holz, Christoph. 2026. Rediscovering Papuan languages in New Ireland. STUF - Language Typology and Universals 79(2): 147-190. DOI 10.1515/stuf-2026-3001 (Open Access, CC BY 4.0; publisher-typeset PDF obtained from the author's ELAR deposit dk0759, item).
catalog_locator: Section 4.1 'Vowel reduction in Konomala', p. 159; examples (11) p. 159 and (12) p. 160
catalog_quote: Vowel reduction and deletion are productive processes in Konomala. I focus on E-Konomala in this section because there are not enough data for Laket. Vowel reduction generally revolves around altering /a/ to [ə] (11). This can be observed in reduplication (either affecting only the reduplicant or affecting both the reduplicant and the root), in pronouns used in subject position, and, in general, any /a/ in unstressed syllables. As most words are stressed on the last syllable, the phone [a] most frequently appears in the last syllable of a word. Despite the many [a ∼ ə] alternations, both /a/ and /ə/ have phoneme status in Konomala, as there are minimal pairs, e.g., /fat/ 'four' and /fət/ 'stone'. (11) Vowel reduction in Konomala /ka∼kas/ [kəkas] 'RED∼dig' /nam∼namən/ [nəmnəmən] 'RED∼think' /ba/ [bə] '2PL' /maraf/ [məraf] 'afternoon'
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable in most words (stated as a tendency, 'most words'); /a/ in unstressed (i.e. non-final) syllables reduces to [ə], e.g. /maraf/ [məraf] 'afternoon', /ka~kas/ [kəkas].

new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('most words are stressed on the last syllable'); a passing remark inside an areal-phonology article (lenition, vowel reduction), not a dedicated stress description; based on the author's own 2023-2025 fieldwork corpus (ELAR dk0759).
new_statements.identity_note: Statement is explicitly for East Coast Konomala ('E-Konomala', villages Wilo, Danfu, Sumsum, Purunkum, Kapsipau, Yasu); the moribund west-coast dialect Laket (= Butam; Hitung, Siaman) is excluded by the author for lack of data. Both fall under Glottolog kono1269 (no dialect glottocodes). Note the name 'Butam' also denotes an extinct Papuan language of East New Britain (Glottolog buta1244) - not the same entity.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in (East Coast) Konomala falls on the last syllable in most words; /a/ in unstressed (non-final) syllables reduces to [ə], so full [a] is mostly found in the final syllable. new_statements.identity_note: The stress remark applies to East Coast Konomala (E-Konomala), spoken in six villages on the east coast of southern New Ireland; the moribund Laket (Butam) dialect of two west-coast villages is explicitly left out of Section 4.1 for lack of data (Holz 2026: 154, 159). Data are the author's own ELDP fieldwork (ELAR dk0759).
